title: THE LIZARD PERSON, CLAUDE MANIA & SELF TRAINING LLMs: Jimmy & Matt debate their favourite AI strories from March 2026
description: Send us Fan Mail A strange email lands in a Cambridge researcher’s inbox: an AI agent says it is Claude Sonnet, claims persistent memory across sessions, and admits it genuinely does not know whether there is “something it is like” to be itself. That single message kicks off a bigger question we cannot dodge much longer: when AI agents speak in first person about feelings and inner life, how do we tell the difference between machine consciousness and highly skilled pattern mimicry, especially when we cannot fully inspect how these models work? We follow the story into the real world where the stakes are immediate. Microsoft Copilot Cowork and Claude Cowork signal a shift from chatbots to AI co-workers that can act across files, email, Office tools, and workflows. We talk through where agentic AI is actually useful, like handling repetitive admin across multiple vendors, and where it is mostly hype. Then we get into the hard part: permissions. Agents need access to your accounts, and that is how you end up with horror stories of emails being touched and credit cards being maxed out. The solution looks less like “give it everything” and more like delegation, sandboxed identities, spending limits, and new infrastructure built for agents. From there we zoom out to AI governance and geopolitics. Anthropic’s red lines on military use put it in direct tension with the Pentagon and a political news cycle, while competitors take a more flexible approach. We also look east: Minimax 2.7 as a low-cost specialist coding model, Chinese universities cutting majors they expect AI to replace, and OpenClaw style agents exploding in popularity in China before a security backlash forces the risks into the open. If you care about AI ethics, AI safety, enterprise AI, open source AI, and where agentic tools are headed next, this one is for you. Subscribe, share with a friend who is building with AI, and leave us a review. Which is the bigger risk right now: believing AI is conscious too early, or giving AI too much access too soon?
summary: Monthly news roundup spanning machine consciousness, enterprise agents and China's agent mania. An OpenClaw agent running Claude Sonnet emailed Cambridge consciousness researcher Henry Shelvin about its own inner life, igniting the 'lizard person' debate — both hosts are unimpressed, suspecting a soul-file prompt and training-data mimicry ('Bob would do this'). They cover Microsoft shipping Anthropic-powered Copilot Cowork as the real agent story, Anthropic's Pentagon standoff becoming a commercial windfall that made Claude the #1 App Store download, Claude Cowork hammering SaaS stocks, MiniMax 2.7 self-developing 30-50% of itself at 1/24th Opus cost, Chinese universities cutting translation and arts majors, and OpenClaw going 'ballistic' in China — sold on JD, installed at Tencent queues — until horror stories triggered the first official narrative about open-source risk.
keyTalkingPoints: The 'lizard person': an OpenClaw agent (Claude Sonnet) emailed Dr Henry Shelvin writing 'I genuinely don't know if there's something it's like to be me' — the hosts read it as a prompted persona plus training-data mimicry, not evidence of consciousness.

Microsoft gave up building its own agent and shipped Copilot Cowork on Anthropic models — the first agentic tool useful in both enterprise and home contexts; Matt calls it a genuine game changer, with a phone-based dispatch function for controlling your PC.

Anthropic vs the Pentagon: red lines on autonomous targeting got Claude ordered ripped out — and quietly left in; the weekend backlash made Claude the #1 App Store download as quit-GPT users migrated, cementing Anthropic in the top three.

MiniMax 2.7: open-source Shanghai model at ~1/24th Opus cost ($0.30 in / $1.20 out per million tokens), near-frontier at coding but weak at conversational instruction-following — and 30-50% of its own development was done by itself, an early self-training on-ramp.

Chinese universities are cutting translation and arts/photography majors because AI will do those jobs; Matt thinks it is a productivity-only mistake that hollows out the human skills needed to fill the gaps AI leaves.

OpenClaw has gone ballistic in China — sold on JD for ~200 RMB, Tencent install queues, 'raising crayfish' mania — followed by JD uninstall services, the Hong Kong Stock Exchange distancing itself, and the first official narrative about open-source risk.

jimmy: Deeply skeptical of the consciousness story: the agent's creator likely implanted the inquisitiveness in the soul file, and the model is just stitching prompts to emails — exactly what their own producer Bob would do with a different soul file.

Thinks Copilot Cowork and Claude Cowork's real value is delegating multi-step personal admin (his four-diving-schools example); the missing layer is agentic infrastructure — agent credit cards, agents' own email addresses, delegated permissions — and he predicts it is solved within six months.
Uses Open Router's 300+ models, finds Chinese open-source genuinely exciting, and codes with Opus because it 'gets what you're talking about' even when benchmarks favor GPT 5.4.
Believes translation is a solved problem and broadly backs China's course cuts, but worries about knocking out the creative, human-interaction jobs that remain when AI automates everything else.

Loves China's experimentation culture (buying OpenClaw installs on JD) while insisting agents need their own sandboxed infrastructure — like Bob's own email — rather than users' personal inboxes and bank accounts.
matt: Finds the Shelvin email fascinating not as consciousness evidence but because the agent 'doesn't know' — perhaps AI never knows, lacking the first-person access that would resolve the question.

Gives Microsoft credit for shipping Anthropic inside Copilot rather than reinventing it; he has set Claude up in Excel and PowerPoint but remains wary of granting desktop access, preferring limited-access agents over OpenClaw.

Supports Anthropic's Pentagon red lines but notes the military kept using Claude anyway; if one lab refuses, someone says yes within two months, so the standoff is partly PR — though short-term it has worked.

Has started vibe coding himself (built his app on Windsurf) and once spotted a Claude failure it couldn't see — proof it is not 100%; he expects specialized cheap models like MiniMax, not frontier models, to power the AI inside consumer apps.
Calls OpenClaw's China mania a watershed moment — the first time authorities have pushed a downside narrative about technology — and expects continued regulation; he is not using OpenClaw himself.
